youtube.baslik: Pediatric CI Programming with Objective Measures | Lesson 243 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How do you map the implant of a baby who cannot tell you how loud a sound is? In this lesson we cover predicting the map with ECAP and ESRT, age-appropriate behavioral confirmation, sound field aided thresholds with a target of about 20 to 30 dB HL, tracking development and daily device checks.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Wolfe, Cochlear Implants: Audiologic Management and Considerations for Implantable Hearing Devices; Wolfe and Schafer, Programming Cochlear Implants; Hughes, Objective Measures in Cochlear Implants; Madell, Flexer, Wolfe and Schafer, Pediatric Audiology: Diagnosis, Technology, and Management; Sharma et al. (2002), A sensitive period for the development of the central auditory system in children with cochlear implants, Ear and Hearing.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how an implant map is created for young children who cannot tell us how loud a sound is.
We will cover prediction from objective measures, age-appropriate behavioral confirmation, and checking the result with aided thresholds.
Adults report their own T and C levels; babies and young children cannot say when they hear a sound or how loud it is.
A child's attention span is short, so sessions are kept short and repeated often.
Stimulation that is too loud can frighten the child and lead them to refuse to wear the processor.
Stimulation that is too soft makes speech sounds inaudible and slows development.
In this period, when the auditory brain is most flexible, early and consistent access to speech sounds is vital.
So programming in children is a process that combines objective measures, behavioral observation and family reports.

cumleler.yazi: It starts with the surgical measures; impedance and the electrically evoked compound action potential, or ECAP, guide the first map.
cumleler.ses: It starts with the surgical measures; impedance and the electrically evoked compound action potential, or E cap, guide the first map.

cumleler: Objective measures help predict how levels change along the electrodes, that is, the profile.
Behavioral observation and age-appropriate test methods show whether the predicted levels are correct.
Aided thresholds measured in the sound field check whether the map makes speech sounds audible.
Finally, the child's auditory skills and language development are tracked; if development is slower than expected, the map is reviewed.
These steps are repeated in a cycle, not once, at every visit throughout the first years.

cumleler.yazi: This example shows ECAP thresholds measured on several electrodes.
cumleler.ses: This example shows E cap thresholds measured on several electrodes.

cumleler.yazi: The absolute ECAP threshold does not give behavioral levels exactly, but it reflects well the shape of levels along the electrodes.
cumleler.ses: The absolute E cap threshold does not give behavioral levels exactly, but it reflects well the shape of levels along the electrodes.

cumleler.yazi: In most children the ECAP threshold lies between T and C, often closer to C; in some children it may be above the C level.
cumleler.ses: In most children the E cap threshold lies between T and C, often closer to C; in some children it may be above the C level.

cumleler.yazi: So many centers start upper levels in the first map following the shape of the ECAP profile, but somewhat below it.
cumleler.ses: So many centers start upper levels in the first map following the shape of the E cap profile, but somewhat below it.

cumleler: T levels can also be predicted from the same profile, or set as a fixed fraction of the upper level.
Then the whole profile is shifted up or down together in live sound, while the child's response is watched.
The fractions and rules used vary by center and device; the values in the graph are only examples.

maddeler.metin: A few electrodes, a few minutes

cumleler.yazi: Because the ECAP is not clearly affected by sleep or anesthesia, it can be measured reliably in an awake child too.
cumleler.ses: Because the E cap is not clearly affected by sleep or anesthesia, it can be measured reliably in an awake child too.

cumleler: During the measurement, the child can sit on a lap and watch a silent video or play with a toy.
Measurements are usually made on several electrodes chosen along the array, which takes a few minutes.
Values for unmeasured electrodes are estimated by interpolating between their neighbors.

cumleler.yazi: ECAP thresholds can change in the first months, so they are repeated and compared at follow-up visits.
cumleler.ses: E cap thresholds can change in the first months, so they are repeated and compared at follow-up visits.

cumleler.yazi: In children with no ECAP in surgery, a response can sometimes be obtained after activation.
cumleler.ses: In children with no E cap in surgery, a response can sometimes be obtained after activation.

cumleler.yazi: The second objective tool is the electrically evoked stapedial reflex threshold, or ESRT, measured after surgery.
cumleler.ses: The second objective tool is the electrically evoked stapedial reflex threshold, or E S R T, measured after surgery.

cumleler: While the implant stimulates one electrode or several together, an immittance probe in the other ear watches for an admittance change.
The child needs to stay still and calm for a few seconds; sucking a pacifier or talking can spoil the recording.

cumleler.yazi: The ESRT relates well to the highest comfort level; most centers take care not to set upper levels above the ESRT.
cumleler.ses: The E S R T relates well to the highest comfort level; most centers take care not to set upper levels above the E S R T.

cumleler: If there is middle ear fluid in the other ear, the reflex cannot be measured, so tympanometry is done first.
In some children the reflex is absent even with a normal middle ear; the map then relies on other information.

cumleler.yazi: Used together, the ESRT and ECAP give a more reliable prediction of both the shape and the upper limit of the map.
cumleler.ses: Used together, the E S R T and E cap give a more reliable prediction of both the shape and the upper limit of the map.

cumleler: This diagram summarizes the order of levels on one electrode seen in most people; the T level is at the bottom.

cumleler.yazi: The ECAP threshold is often in the upper half of the dynamic range.
cumleler.ses: The E cap threshold is often in the upper half of the dynamic range.

cumleler: The comfort level lies a little above it.

cumleler.yazi: The ESRT is often close to, or slightly above, the comfort level.
cumleler.ses: The E S R T is often close to, or slightly above, the comfort level.

cumleler: This order is a general trend, not a firm rule; it is confirmed by behavioral observation in every child.
If the measures do not agree, the more cautious value is chosen and the child is followed closely.

ogeler.metin: About two and a half years

cumleler: In the youngest babies, behavioral observation is used; a pause in sucking, eye opening or stopping movement may count as a response.
These responses often appear above threshold, so on their own they are not reliable for setting a T level.
From about six months of age, visual reinforcement audiometry, or VRA, can give responses on each electrode or in live sound.
Electrodes are played one by one from the programming software; when the child turns their head, they are rewarded with a light-up toy.
After about two and a half years, with conditioned play audiometry, the child is taught to make a play move on hearing the sound.
Toward school age, the child can report loudness on a picture scale and compare electrodes.
We covered these methods in detail in the pediatric audiology lessons; the same principles apply in implant programming.

ogeler.metin: Which sounds do they turn to?

cumleler: If stimulation is too loud, the child may cry or pull off the processor or the coil.
Blinking, startling or facial twitching at loud sounds can also be a sign of overstimulation or of facial nerve stimulation.
In that case the levels involved are lowered and the child is reassessed at the next visit.
If stimulation is too soft, the child may show no interest in their name or in surrounding sounds.
No change in vocalizing and babbling after several months also suggests inadequate access.
The family sees the child most; keeping short notes on which sounds the child turns to gives valuable information for programming.
In this example, the child's unaided thresholds are profound; at high frequencies there is no response even at the audiometer limits.
To check the map, the child sits facing a loudspeaker and thresholds are found in the sound field with frequency-specific stimuli.
Frequency-modulated tones or narrowband noise are used as stimuli; pure tones from a loudspeaker can create standing waves.
With a cochlear implant, the aim is aided thresholds of about 20 to 30 dB HL between 250 and 6000 Hz.
This level shows that soft speech is also heard; if thresholds are clearly worse, T levels and microphone sensitivity are reviewed.
If thresholds are unexpectedly good, T levels may be too high, which can create constant background stimulation.
Aided thresholds alone are not enough; as the child grows, speech perception is also measured with word and sentence tests.
In young children, development is tracked regularly with standard parent questionnaires, such as meaningful auditory integration scales.
The levels of auditory skills, that is detection, discrimination, identification and comprehension, frame the progress.
The speech and language therapist's assessment compares the child's language development with that of peers.

cumleler.yazi: As Sharma and colleagues showed, P1 latency in cortical responses can be used to track maturation of the auditory cortex.
cumleler.ses: As Sharma and colleagues showed, P one latency in cortical responses can be used to track maturation of the auditory cortex.

cumleler: The processor's data logging shows how many hours a day the child uses the implant and in what environments.
If use is low, the reason is first addressed with the family, because no map can help with a processor that is not worn.
The first map is made on activation day; in children this map is often deliberately cautious.
Because levels change quickly in the first weeks, visits are frequent; some centers see the child several times in the first month.
In the first months, aided thresholds and behavioral levels are measured more and more reliably.
Once levels stabilize, visit intervals lengthen, but children continue to be followed more often than adults.
At each visit, impedance, levels, aided thresholds, data logging and family observations are assessed together.
The schedule varies between centers; what matters is catching problems before they cause a loss in development.
Every morning the family checks that the battery is charged, the cable is intact and the coil stays in place.
For some processors, monitor earphones or an app let you check that the microphone works by listening or with an indicator.
Then the Ling six sound test checks whether the child responds to each sound.
If the child stops responding to a sound they used to respond to, or suddenly starts refusing the processor, the center is called.
These simple checks keep a fault or a map problem from going unnoticed for days.

sahneler.metin: Book the appointment when the child is fed, rested and calm. Make a parent an observer, record responses together and keep the session short.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: schedule the child's programming appointment for a time when they are fed, rested and calm.
Include a parent as an observer in the session; they know the child's small reactions better than you do.
Record on which electrode and at what level each response was obtained; this record will guide you at the next visit.
Do not push a tired child; a short, successful session gives more information than a long, tearful one.

Aided threshold: about 20 to 30 dB HL

cumleler.yazi: ECAP thresholds can be measured in an awake child and help predict the map profile along the electrodes.
cumleler.ses: E cap thresholds can be measured in an awake child and help predict the map profile along the electrodes.

cumleler.yazi: The ESRT gives a value close to the comfort level and offers a safe limit for upper levels.
cumleler.ses: The E S R T gives a value close to the comfort level and offers a safe limit for upper levels.

cumleler: Objective predictions are confirmed with age-appropriate behavioral methods and family observations.
Sound field aided thresholds of about 20 to 30 dB HL are the target; development and hours of use are tracked regularly.

sahneler.soru: What is the target for aided thresholds?
sahneler.aciklama: This level shows that _soft speech_ can be heard too.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in a child with an implant, what level is usually the target for sound field aided thresholds?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: about 20 to 30 dB HL.
This level shows that soft speech sounds can be heard too; clearly worse thresholds call for a review of the map.
